newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU ruling boosts Italy's bid for single currency.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU ruling boosts Italy's bid for single currency.

text.p: The European Union on Friday bolstered Italy's hopes of a timely entry into a single currency by approving its controversial euro-tax, a one-off measure aimed at bringing its public finances under control in 1997.
Eurostat, the EU's statistical office, said the "the Italian tax on wage funds is a new tax and should be recorded as a receipt reducing the deficit."
Italy, like other EU states, is trying to bring its deficit, debt and other budget targets into line with criteria set in the EU's Maastricht treaty for qualifying for the EU's single currency.

In Rome, the Italian Treasury welcomed the decision, but the German finance ministry, where there is concern about Italy's fitness to be a founding member of the new euro currency, declined to comment.
Eurostat estimated that the part of the so-called euro-tax it was reviewing would represent 0.19 percent of GDP.

The estimated amount to be collected under that portion of the tax is 3.5 trillion lire ($2.1 billion), the office added. This is less than the 5.5 trillion lire analysts had originally anticipated would be covered under the ruling.

European Commission officials stressed that the remaining portion of the tax -- 0.4 percent of GDP -- was not under dispute in this latest review. Therefore the entire tax, roughly 12.0 trillion lire and representing about 0.6 percent of GDP, can now be applied towards the 1997 budget deficit.
When the tax was initially proposed by Rome it came under fire from critics who saw it as a temporary measure and not in line with durable budgetary consolidation.
Moreover, early statements from Italian politicians suggested the levy might be reimbursed to taxpayers once Rome qualified for monetary union.
But EU officials stressed on Friday that there was no mention of the possiblity of repayment in Italy's proposal.
"We examined Italy's financial act and found nowhere a committment to repay it," an EU official told a news conference.
Had such a promise been included, the EU would have ruled against the tax, he added.
Commission officials, meanwhile, cautioned against taking today's ruling and extrapolating what the EU executive might forecast for Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio in 1997.

The Commission will revise its economic and budget forecasts for the entire 15-nation bloc in April. At that time it will assess the effects of Eurostat's rulings as well as the economic conditions in Italy.
In addition, meeting Maastricht's target for budget deficits was only one part of demonstrating sustainable economic convergence.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday that the government was currently some six to 14 trillion lire ($3.6-$8.4 billion) short of the Maastricht deficit target.
Earlier this week Rome has said it will have to put in place a new mini-budget to deal with the anticipated revenue shortfall.

Regarding the treatment of state guarantees for Italy's railway system, Eurostat ruled that "public enterprises' debt guaranteed by the state should be directly taken into account in the government debt.
This final verdict would allow Italy's 1997 deficit to decline by 0.2 percent of GDP.
($ = 1663 Italian Lire)
